name: Christian Shaw
social_status: Daughter of John Shaw, Laird of Bargarran; landed gentry
biography:
Christian Shaw was the eleven-year-old daughter of the Laird of Bargarran in Renfrewshire, Scotland, whose alleged bewitchment in 1696-1697 led to one of the last major Scottish witch prosecutions and resulted in seven executions in June 1697. Shaw began experiencing fits and strange symptoms in August 1696, initially attributed to natural causes, but her subsequent claims that she was being tormented by named individuals triggered an investigation that rapidly expanded under the attention of physicians, ministers, and eventually the Privy Council.

Shaw's accusations implicated individuals from a range of social backgrounds, and her performances of affliction — convulsions, vomiting of feathers, pins, and hay, apparent trances — were witnessed by credible and educated observers including physicians who initially found them inexplicable. The case drew national attention and was referred to the Privy Council. A commission tried twenty-four individuals, of whom seven were convicted and hanged and burned on the Gallow Green in Paisley on June 10, 1697.

In a remarkable biographical turn, Christian Shaw survived to adulthood and around 1720 founded the Bargarran Thread Company in Johnstone, Renfrewshire, using spinning techniques she had observed or developed. The thread company became economically significant and her later life as a successful businesswoman stands in sharp contrast to her childhood role as the center of a lethal witch prosecution. Historians debate whether Shaw's fits were genuine psychosomatic illness, deliberate performance, or some combination, but the debate itself illustrates the impossibility of distinguishing between these categories in early modern contexts.
arrest_narrative: Christian Shaw was not arrested but rather was the accuser in the Bargarran case. Her symptoms of affliction beginning in August 1696 were formally investigated after she began naming her tormentors. The accused were arrested based primarily on her testimony.

interrogation_and_confession.initial_response: Presented as victim of bewitchment, not as accused
interrogation_and_confession.final_confession_summary: Not applicable — Shaw was the accuser; her testimony named seven individuals who were subsequently executed, plus additional accused who survived

accusations_against_them: Not accused — role as accuser: claimed bewitchment by seven neighbors
Testimony resulted in seven executions on Gallow Green, Paisley, June 10, 1697
historiographical_significance: Shaw's case is one of the most studied of the later Scottish witch prosecutions both for the quality of documentation and for the remarkable trajectory of her subsequent life. Her founding of the Bargarran Thread Company has been used to argue either that she was a calculating individual who used witch accusation instrumentally, or that her survival and business success were unrelated to the childhood episode. Historians including Michael Wasser have analyzed the case for evidence of how child accusers operated in Scottish prosecution dynamics.
source_method: A True Narrative of the Sufferings and Relief of a Young Girl (1698, contemporary pamphlet); Privy Council records; discussed in Goodare's Scottish Witch-Hunt in Context (2002)
